title: What Is the Score Actually Made Of?
scopeNote: This keeps the decomposition and the comparison with a task the person never trained. The second is what makes the first testable rather than a taxonomy: the untrained task can only rise by the restitution band. Five simulated people, the staged experiments on each contribution separately, and the treatment of plateaus stay in the longer version.
summary: A fictional patient's score on a practised task climbs over two years. Four contributions with different time courses are stacked underneath it, and a task they never practised rises only by the restitution band, so the gap is everything that did not generalise.
learningObjectives: Separate restitution, relearning, compensation and practice as contributions to a rising score.
Explain why only restitution shows up on a task that was never trained.
Explain why an untrained task is worth more than another session on the trained one.
Recognise that a large, steady improvement can generalise almost not at all.
State why compensation is a real solution even though it does not generalise.
interactionTypes: four live sliders setting how much each contribution provides
a stacked-band chart with its own time course per contribution
a trained and an untrained task drawn on the same axes
a guided case where a large steady rise generalises by seven per cent
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with each contribution a native range input reporting its value in text. The chart carries a description giving the starting score, all four contributions at two years, both final scores and the gap between them, so the decomposition is fully available as text. The two lines differ by dash pattern as well as by colour and are labelled at their right-hand ends; where they coincide, which happens when everything that contributes is restitution, a single combined label is drawn rather than two on top of each other. The band key runs along the bottom rather than down the gutter, so it cannot collide with the line labels at any setting. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: A simulation with invented time courses. No real patient, trajectory or rehabilitation outcome is described.
simulationNotes: Each contribution has its own saturating time course: restitution is fast and largely done by six months, relearning climbs steadily and is still rising at two years, compensation is slow to start because a strategy has to be found first, and the practice effect appears immediately and stays flat. The trained task is the base plus all four; the untrained task is the base plus restitution only. The guided case sets restitution to 4 and the other three high, producing a climb from 20 to 80 over two years of which only seven per cent generalises, which is the demonstration. The caution states that the contributions are not separable or additive in reality, that relearning and restitution interact, that compensation can itself drive neural change, that the time courses are illustrative shapes rather than measured ones, and that a genuinely untrained task sharing the same function is hard to find.
readmeTopic: what a rising recovery score is actually made of, and how much of it generalises
